ap_statistics-m01.stem: A nutritionist wants to know whether a new diet changes the mean weight loss compared with a standard diet. In each of $14$ randomly selected pairs of twins, one twin is randomly assigned to each diet. A dotplot of the $14$ differences (new diet minus standard diet) is strongly right-skewed with an outlier, and a dotplot of the $14$ weight losses on the new diet is roughly symmetric with no outliers. Which of the following identifies the appropriate $t$ procedure to compare the means and states whether its normality condition is met?

options.text: Two-sample $t$ procedure; the normality condition is met, because the dotplot of the $14$ weight losses on the new diet is roughly symmetric with no outliers
options.why: Treats the two sets of measurements as two independent samples although the same individuals (or matched pairs) produced both sets.

options.text: Matched-pairs $t$ procedure; the normality condition is met, because the dotplot of the $14$ weight losses on the new diet is roughly symmetric with no outliers
options.why: Checks the shape of one set of measurements instead of the shape of the differences.

options.text: Matched-pairs $t$ procedure; the normality condition is not met, because the values before and after are dependent
options.why: The pairs are meant to be dependent; the normality condition is about the shape of the differences, not about independence of the two measurements.

options.text: Matched-pairs $t$ procedure; the normality condition is not met, because there are only $14$ differences and they are strongly right-skewed with an outlier
options.why: The pairs are the units, so the differences must be checked: $14 < 30$ and their dotplot is strongly skewed, so the condition is not met.

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A random sample of $25$ bags of coffee gives a $95\%$ confidence interval of $(10.7, 11.5)$ for $\mu$, the mean weight, in ounces, of all bags of coffee filled by a machine. The same sample is used to test $H_0: \mu = 11.7$ against $H_a: \mu \ne 11.7$ at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$. Assume that the conditions for inference are met. Which of the following is a correct conclusion?

options.text: Fail to reject $H_0$; there is not convincing evidence that $\mu \ne 11.7$
options.why: Places $11.7$ inside the interval, but it lies outside $(10.7, 11.5)$.

options.text: No conclusion can be reached, because a confidence interval cannot be used to carry out a significance test
options.why: Treats the interval and the test as unrelated, but a two-sided interval at confidence level $1-\alpha$ gives the decision for a two-sided test at level $\alpha$.

options.text: Fail to reject $H_0$; there is convincing evidence that $\mu = 11.7$
options.why: Failing to reject $H_0$ never gives evidence that $H_0$ is true.

options.text: Reject $H_0$; there is convincing evidence that $\mu \ne 11.7$
options.why: The $95\%$ interval matches a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$, and $11.7$ is outside $(10.7, 11.5)$, so $H_0$ is rejected (the P-value is about $0.005$).

blueprint.concept: Use a confidence interval to reach the decision of a matching significance test, including the direction of a one-sided alternative
student_thinking: Match the confidence level of the interval to the significance level and the sidedness of the test
Locate the hypothesized value relative to the interval and relative to the direction of the alternative hypothesis
Turn the location into a decision about $H_0$ and state the conclusion about the claim without accepting the null hypothesis

key_conditions.condition: a two-sided interval at confidence level $1-2\alpha$ matches a one-sided test at level $\alpha$, and a two-sided interval at level $1-\alpha$ matches a two-sided test
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the interval, the null value, the alternative and the significance level

misconceptions.description: believes an interval cannot give a test decision
misplaces the null value or ignores the direction of the alternative
treats failing to reject as evidence that the null hypothesis is true

verification.independent_path: the decision is found from the position of the null value in the rounded interval and again from the t statistic and P-value (scipy and a numerically integrated t cdf), and the two must agree with a margin from the significance level

steps: Match the confidence level of the interval to the significance level and the sidedness of the test
Locate the hypothesized value relative to the interval and relative to the direction of the alternative hypothesis
Turn the location into a decision about $H_0$ and state the conclusion about the claim without accepting the null hypothesis
concepts: duality of confidence intervals and significance tests
decision wording and direction of the alternative hypothesis

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A random sample of $17$ commuters gives a $95\%$ confidence interval of $(20.8, 27.6)$ for $\mu$, the mean time, in minutes, that all commuters in a city spend on the way to work. The same sample is used to test $H_0: \mu = 29.8$ against $H_a: \mu > 29.8$ at significance level $\alpha = 0.025$. Assume that the conditions for inference are met. Which of the following is a correct conclusion?

options.text: No conclusion can be reached, because a confidence interval cannot be used to carry out a significance test
options.why: Treats the interval and the test as unrelated, but a two-sided interval at confidence level $1-2\alpha$ gives the decision for a test at level $\alpha$ in the direction supported by the interval.

options.text: Reject $H_0$; there is convincing evidence that $\mu > 29.8$
options.why: Sees $29.8$ outside the interval but ignores which side supports $H_a$.

options.text: Fail to reject $H_0$; there is not convincing evidence that $\mu > 29.8$
options.why: A $95\%$ two-sided interval matches a one-sided test at $\alpha = 0.025$; $29.8$ lies above the interval, on the side opposite to the alternative, so the sample gives no support for $H_a$ and $H_0$ is not rejected (the P-value is about $0.998$).

options.text: Reject $H_0$; there is convincing evidence that $\mu < 29.8$
options.why: Rejects in the direction opposite to the alternative hypothesis, which the test does not support.

ap_statistics-m03.stem: The population distribution of the amount of time, in minutes, that customers wait to be served at a bank is approximately normal, with mean $\mu = 72$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 20$. One random sample of $25$ observations from this population has a sample mean of $75$. Consider the sample means of all possible random samples of size $25$ from this population. Which of the following describes the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar{x}$?

options.text: Mean $72$, standard deviation $4$, skewed to the right
options.why: Requires a sample size of at least $30$ even though the population is already approximately normal.

options.text: Mean $72$, standard deviation $4$, approximately normal
options.why: The mean of $\bar{x}$ is $\mu=72$, the standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 20/\sqrt{25} = 4$. The population is approximately normal, so the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal for every sample size.

options.text: Mean $75$, standard deviation $4$, approximately normal
options.why: Centers the sampling distribution at the mean of the one sample that was observed instead of at the population mean.

options.text: Mean $72$, standard deviation $0.8$, approximately normal
options.why: Divides the population standard deviation by $n$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}$.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Describe the center, spread and shape of the sampling distribution of a sample mean from the population and the sample size
student_thinking: Identify the center of the sampling distribution as the population mean, not the mean of the one observed sample
Compute the standard deviation of the sample mean as the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size
Use the shape of the population and the sample size to decide whether the Central Limit Theorem makes the sampling distribution approximately normal

key_conditions.condition: the sampling distribution of the mean has mean mu, standard deviation sigma over root n, and is approximately normal when the population is normal or the sample size is large
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the population shape, mean and standard deviation, the sample size and one observed sample mean

misconceptions.description: centers the distribution at the one observed sample mean
forgets to divide by the square root of the sample size
applies or withholds the Central Limit Theorem incorrectly

verification.independent_path: the standard deviation of a mean of n independent observations is recomputed from the variance of a weighted sum with numpy and compared with the closed form; the shape follows from a table of (population shape, sample size)
verification.method: variance of a weighted sum and shape table

ap_statistics-m03.stem: The population distribution of the weight, in pounds, of the luggage checked by passengers on a flight is strongly skewed to the right, with mean $\mu = 60$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 12$. One random sample of $16$ observations from this population has a sample mean of $57$. Consider the sample means of all possible random samples of size $16$ from this population. Which of the following describes the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar{x}$?

options.text: Mean $60$, standard deviation $3$, approximately normal
options.why: Applies the Central Limit Theorem to a sample size that is too small for it when the population is strongly skewed.

options.text: Mean $60$, standard deviation $3$, skewed to the right
options.why: The mean of $\bar{x}$ is $\mu=60$, the standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 12/\sqrt{16} = 3$. The population is strongly skewed and $16 < 30$, so the Central Limit Theorem does not apply and the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is still skewed to the right.

options.text: Mean $60$, standard deviation $0.75$, skewed to the right
options.why: Divides the population standard deviation by $n$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}$.

options.text: Mean $57$, standard deviation $3$, skewed to the right
options.why: Centers the sampling distribution at the mean of the one sample that was observed instead of at the population mean.

ap_statistics-m04.stem: A least-squares regression line is used to predict the selling price of the car from the age of a car (in years), using $20$ observations. The residual plot is shown, and the coefficient of determination is $r^2 = 0.48$. A student says that a linear model is not appropriate because $r^2 = 0.48$ is small. Which of the following is the best response to the student?

stimulus.description: Residual plot with a horizontal line at zero

options.text: The linear model is appropriate, because the residuals add up to $0$
options.why: Reaches the right decision for the wrong reason: least-squares residuals always add up to $0$, whatever the model.

options.text: The linear model is appropriate, because the residual plot shows no pattern; the small $r^2$ means only that the model explains $48\%$ of the variation in the response
options.why: The residuals scatter randomly about $0$ with no pattern, so the linear model is appropriate; $r^2 = 0.48$ says the line explains about $48\%$ of the variation but does not mean the form is wrong.

options.text: The linear model is not appropriate, because the residual plot shows a curved pattern that the line does not capture
options.why: Misreads the residual plot: the residuals are randomly scattered, not curved.

options.text: The linear model is not appropriate, because an $r^2$ below $0.60$ shows that the relationship is not linear
options.why: Treats a small $r^2$ as evidence that the form is not linear; a linear relationship with a lot of scatter can have a small $r^2$.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Assess a linear model from the residual plot and a stated r squared, and respond to a claim that uses r squared as the criterion
student_thinking: Read the residual plot for a systematic pattern such as a curve rather than random scatter about zero
Recognize that the size of $r^2$ measures the share of variation explained and does not decide whether a linear form is appropriate
State the decision about the linear model with the residual pattern as the evidence

key_conditions.condition: the form of the relationship is judged from the residual pattern, while r squared only measures the share of variation explained
key_conditions.evidence: the stem shows the residual plot, gives r squared and states a student's claim

misconceptions.description: sees random scatter in a curve or a curve in random scatter
uses the size of r squared as proof or disproof of linearity
gives the right decision with a reason that is true of every model

verification.independent_path: residuals are made orthogonal to x like least-squares residuals; a quadratic fit R squared and the correlation of absolute residuals with x classify the pattern, which must match the intended pattern

steps: Read the residual plot for a systematic pattern such as a curve rather than random scatter about zero
Recognize that the size of $r^2$ measures the share of variation explained and does not decide whether a linear form is appropriate
State the decision about the linear model with the residual pattern as the evidence
concepts: residual plot as evidence about the form of the model
interpretation of the coefficient of determination

ap_statistics-m05.stem: The scatterplot shown displays $12$ observations of the number of hours of sleep and a reaction time score (in milliseconds). The point circled in red is removed, and the correlation coefficient and the least-squares line are recomputed. Which of the following best describes the effect of removing the point?

options.text: The correlation becomes stronger and the slope of the least-squares line becomes noticeably steeper
options.why: Misjudges what kind of point the circled point is: it treats a point of one type (extreme in $x$ and on the trend, extreme in $x$ and off the trend, or extreme only in $y$) as if it were another type.

options.text: The correlation becomes stronger and the slope of the least-squares line becomes about the same
options.why: Without the circled point $|r|$ changes from $0.69$ to $0.98$ and the slope magnitude from $2.83$ to $2.69$.

options.text: The correlation becomes weaker and the slope of the least-squares line becomes about the same
options.why: Gets the effect on the correlation backwards: the point lies away from the line and pulls the correlation down, so without it the correlation is stronger.

options.text: The correlation becomes stronger and the slope of the least-squares line becomes noticeably less steep
options.why: Gets the effect on the slope wrong: the point is near the middle of the $x$-values, so removing it leaves the slope about the same.

student_thinking: Classify the circled point by its position: far from the other $x$-values (leverage) or only far in the $y$-direction, and on or off the trend of the other points

Decide whether removing a point of that type changes the slope of the least-squares line noticeably

ap_statistics-m06.stem: A researcher tests $H_0: \mu = 70$ versus $H_a: \mu > 70$, where $\mu$ is the mean score of all students at a school on a reading test, using a random sample of students from a population that is approximately normal with a known standard deviation of $15$. The table shows the power of the test against the alternative $\mu = 74$ for several sample sizes and significance levels. The researcher currently uses $n = 25$ and $\alpha = 0.05$ and is considering a change to $n = 100$ and $\alpha = 0.01$. Which of the following describes the effect of the change?

stimulus.description: Power of the test against the alternative mean for several sample sizes and significance levels

data.title: Power of the test against the alternative mean 74

options.text: The probability of a Type I error increases and the power of the test decreases
options.why: Gets the Type I error backwards and also reads the change in power in the wrong direction.

options.text: The probability of a Type I error decreases and the power of the test increases
options.why: The probability of a Type I error equals the significance level, so it goes from $0.05$ to $0.01$; the table shows the power changing from $0.38$ to $0.63$.

options.text: The probability of a Type I error decreases and the power of the test decreases
options.why: Lets one of the two changes dominate: the table shows the net change in power from $0.38$ to $0.63$, which is the other direction.

options.text: The probability of a Type I error increases and the power of the test increases
options.why: Gets the Type I error backwards: its probability equals the new significance level, so it follows the change in the significance level, not the sample size.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Judge the combined effect on the Type I error probability and the power of changing the significance level and the sample size together, using a table of powers
student_thinking: Recall that the probability of a Type I error equals the significance level, so it follows the change in $\alpha$
Locate the current and the proposed combination of sample size and significance level in the power table

ap_statistics-m07.stem: A bag contains $8$ red marbles and $5$ blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random, one after the other, without replacement. The tree diagram shows the probabilities of the first and second draws. Given that the second marble is red, what is the probability that the first marble was blue? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Probability tree for two draws without replacement

options.why: Finds the probability that the first is blue and the second is red but does not divide by the probability of the given event.
Reports the overall probability that the second draw is red, which is the denominator rather than the conditional probability.
Reads the branch probability for the second draw given the first, which reverses the conditional probability that is asked for.
Add the two paths whose second draw is red: the probability of that event is $0.6154$; the path through blue first has probability $0.2564$, so the answer is $0.2564/0.6154 \approx 0.417$.

ap_statistics-m08.stem: Suppose that $60\%$ of the $40000$ registered voters in a large city support a proposed tax. A simple random sample of $200$ of them is selected, and $\hat{p}$ is the proportion of the sample who support a proposed tax. Which of the following is the best statement about the conditions for a normal model for $\hat{p}$ and about $P(\hat{p} < 0.66)$? Round the probability to three decimal places.

options.text: The conditions are met, and the probability is approximately $0.549$
options.why: Uses $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ as the standard deviation of $\hat{p}$ without dividing by $\sqrt{n}$.

options.text: The conditions are met, and the probability is approximately $0.042$
options.why: Finds the probability in the wrong tail: the area to the left of the value is the one asked for.

options.text: The normal model is not appropriate, because the population proportion is not equal to $0.5$
options.why: Treats a population proportion of exactly $0.5$ as a requirement; the large counts condition is that $np$ and $n(1-p)$ are both at least $10$, which holds here.

options.text: The conditions are met, and the probability is approximately $0.958$
options.why: $np = 120$ and $n(1-p) = 80$ are both at least $10$ and the sample is less than $10\%$ of the population, so $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal with mean $0.6$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{0.6(1-0.6)/200} \approx 0.0346$; $z = 1.73$ gives $0.958$.

ap_statistics-m09.stem: An experiment compares two treatments using $60$ patients. The patients were first separated into two blocks, and within each block the treatments were assigned at random so that each treatment was given to $15$ patients. The table summarizes the reduction in blood pressure, in points. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the table and the design?

stimulus.description: Summary of the response by block and treatment

data.title: Summary statistics by block and treatment

options.text: Blocking guarantees that the new exercise program caused the difference of about $6$, so random assignment of the treatments within the blocks was not necessary in this design
options.why: Blocking controls only the blocking variable; random assignment within each block is still needed to balance all other variables.

options.text: The new exercise program works much better in older patients than in younger patients, so the effect of the treatment depends on the block and blocking was not useful in this experiment
options.why: Misreads the table: the treatment means differ by about the same amount ($6.3$ and $5.7$) in the two blocks.

options.text: The difference of about $29$ between the blocks is an effect of the treatments, so the blocks should be ignored and all $60$ patients compared as one group
options.why: Attributes the difference between the blocks to the treatments, although every block received both treatments.

options.text: The reduction in blood pressure differs by about $29$ between the blocks but by only about $6$ between the treatments in each block, so blocking removed the block differences while random assignment within blocks is still needed
options.why: Within each block the treatment means differ by $6.3$ and $5.7$, while the block means differ by about $28.9$ and the standard deviations are small; blocking removes the block-to-block variation, and randomizing within blocks balances the other variables.

ap_statistics-m10.stem: A researcher takes an independent random sample of $100$ students from each of $4$ schools and records the preferred way to get to school of each student in the table shown. The researcher will carry out a chi-square test using these counts. Which of the following gives the appropriate null hypothesis and degrees of freedom?

stimulus.description: Two-way table of school and preferred way to get to school

options.text: $H_0$: the distribution of preferred way to get to school is the same for all $4$ schools; $df = 6$
options.why: Separate random samples were taken from each of the $4$ schools, so this is a test of homogeneity: the null hypothesis says that the distribution of the response is the same in every group; $df = (4-1)(3-1) = 6$.

options.text: $H_0$: the sample proportions of preferred way to get to school are equal for all $4$ schools; $df = 6$
options.why: States the hypothesis about sample proportions in the table; hypotheses are about population parameters, and the sample proportions differ by chance.

options.text: $H_0$: the distribution of preferred way to get to school is the same for all $4$ schools; $df = 11$
options.why: Uses the number of cells minus $1$ for the degrees of freedom instead of $(4-1)(3-1)$.

options.text: $H_0$: school and preferred way to get to school are independent in the population of all students; $df = 6$
options.why: Describes a test of independence, which is for one random sample classified on two variables; here the samples were taken separately from each group.
